item.title: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
item.description:
President Trump called for an investigation into the government's economic statistics on Thursday, alleging without evidence that growth figures released before the midterm elections were deliberately understated.

Why it matters: Revisions to GDP are routine and reflect more complete information that becomes available after the initial estimates are published.

  • The allegations could renew concerns about political interference in the production of critical economic data that underpin trillions of dollars in investment decisions and Federal Reserve policy.

What they're saying: The Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday substantially revised the third-quarter GDP data, reflecting a 4.3% annualized pace of growth, up from the 3.4% reported less than a week before the midterm elections.

  • Trump claimed in a Thanksgiving morning Truth Social post that the initial figures were "FAKE."
  • "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation," Trump wrote in the post, calling it a "massive, and purposeful, error."

The intrigue: Government statistical agencies operate under longstanding standards that are aimed at insulating career economists and statisticians from political influence in the collection and dissemination of economic data.

  • But it's not the first time an agency has come under Trump's fire anyway, following his dismissal of the Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner last year over revisions to jobs data.
  • This time, however, the agency that released GDP and other key economic data is housed within the Commerce Department — led by one of Trump's closest political allies, Howard Lutnick.

Friction point: There is a legitimate debate about how to improve the timeliness and accuracy of government economic data.

  • But that is fundamentally different from Trump's allegation that federal statisticians deliberately misrepresented the strength of the economy.

How it works: The initial GDP figure is not supposed to be definitive. The government revises its estimates as more comprehensive data become available — a process that long predates the Trump administration.

  • Trump also railed against the GDP revision in a separate, wide-ranging Thanksgiving message, calling it a "RECORD SETTING ERROR" and claiming the updated figures came "three weeks late."
  • But the BEA released the revised figures on its previously announced schedule. The agency publishes three estimates of quarterly GDP over three months.

Between the lines: The 0.9 percentage point upward revision revealed yesterday was larger than usual. Historically, the first revision to quarterly growth figures has averaged 0.5 percentage points in either direction.

  • But it was not unprecedented: There was a larger revision during Trump's first term, when the BEA revised second-quarter 2020 GDP growth upward by 1.2 percentage points.
  • The agency's explanation for this larger-than-usual revision: Updated data on software prices and retail sales showed stronger business investment and consumer spending than initially estimated.

Reality check: Unlike the dismal jobs report that drew Trump's ire last year, the initial GDP figures already painted a picture of a booming economy.

  • The upward revision simply made that snapshot even rosier. It also bolsters the case for further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, something Trump opposes.

For the record: The Commerce Department and BEA did not respond immediately to requests for comment.

The bottom line: Federal statisticians face growing presidential scrutiny over revisions to economic data — whether those revisions reveal a weaker economy or an even stronger one.

  • The BEA will publish another estimate of third quarter growth on Dec. 23.

item.title: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
item.description:
Elon Musk on Wednesday pledged two SpaceX shares for every child in America, doubling an offer he made just last month.

Why it matters: The $18 billion-plus giveaway roughly triples Michael Dell's once record-breaking Trump accounts gift.

What they're saying: "Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," he said in a post to X.

  • On Oct. 19, he promised that every child would receive one share next year, adding it would be the "first of many."

By the numbers: With about 72 million minors in the U.S. per Census estimates, and at SpaceX's closing price Wednesday, the gift would be worth around $18.35 billion.

  • Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, and the company has billions of shares outstanding, so the giveaway likely wouldn't have much impact on him or investors.

Yes, but: The stock's fallen about 13% since he made the initial promise, amid a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks.

Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX.

  • In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts.

What's next: Musk did not offer a timing for the new distribution.

item.title: The pros and cons of Medicare for All
item.description:
The boldest idea in health care comes down to one massive tradeoff: Guaranteed coverage for everyone in exchange for an eye-popping price tag and an ultra-messy transition.

Why it matters: Talk of Medicare for All is growing now that Democrats will control Congress next year with huge majorities in both chambers — so it's time to take a clinical look at the pros and cons, based on what we're hearing from policy experts who have studied it.

Driving the news: The idea is getting a fresh round of attention after Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) — a major supporter of Medicare for All who wrote a book about it — offered to name the plan "TrumpCare," complete with gold insurance cards, if President Trump helps pass it.

  • Trump reposted his offer and has offered to meet with El-Sayed, telling the New York Post: "Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go."

Reality check: They will probably meet, and it could end with mutual praise and hopeful vibes (with echoes of Trump's meetings with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani). El-Sayed likes to flatter Trump. Trump likes to be flattered.

  • But don't take that as a sign that a deal is imminent. There's pretty much zero common ground, other than calling it TrumpCare. Trump hates Medicare for All.
  • Trump is all about cutting more drug price deals and sending people money to buy their own coverage — hardly a big government takeover of the health system.

But Democrats can certainly try to force votes on Medicare for All when they're in power, although they're likely to find that not everyone in the party is on board.

  • Medicare for All backers are wagering that enough people are fed up with the existing health system that they'll accept a bigger federal role providing coverage to more Americans, warts and all.
  • "It's no longer [enough] from a political policy point of view to tinker around the edges," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) told reporters last week. "Increasingly, elected officials understand the current health care system is broken."

The pros: Medicare for All would replace the nation's fragmented insurance system with universal coverage that's subject to a single standard.

  • That would, in theory, eliminate the gaps that left 28 million Americans uninsured last year, per most recent Centers for Disease Control figures.
  • The coverage also would be "portable," meaning you'd keep the same arrangement if you change jobs or move to a different state. For life.
  • The basic benefits would also be more generous than in most existing forms of public and private insurance. And with no insurance co-pays and fewer out-of-pocket expenses, some households could come out ahead.

The cons: Sticker shock. The projected 10-year cost of implementing a plan is about $47 trillion, per the White House Council of Economic Advisers, which predicts higher taxes, more deficit spending and program cuts.

  • There's also the transition to a new system. Sanders' 2017 Medicare for All bill called for current workplace coverage, Medicare Advantage, Medigap, Affordable Care Act plans and most existing Medicaid coverage to disappear in four years.
  • How the government would take care of the continuity of people's medical care during that time is a big unknown. (El-Sayed says he's in favor of allowing "additional private insurance through unions or employers" so it's not all wiped out.)
  • Critics predict delays in getting medical tests and treatments — because once there's no more cost sharing, doctors' offices and clinics could get overwhelmed with new patients, possibly diverting care from patients with urgent needs.

Between the lines: Some Democrats are already convinced they're not going to get Medicare for All, so they're looking into narrower changes like lowering the eligibility age for Medicare — although even those ideas could cause headaches of their own.

The bottom line: There's no such thing as "problem solved" in health care — but the Democratic sweep could give voice to the voters who are tired of the current problems and want to try something new.

item.title: Cookbook GPT: When AI becomes a Thanksgiving sous-chef
item.description:
From cookbooks to YouTube to ChatGPT, the way Americans plan their holiday menus has evolved.

The big picture: But there's something uniquely human about building a recipe, and chefs warn we risk fracturing personal connections and family history by reducing culinary traditions to chatbot prompts.

  • "Recipes can have tradition and ritual," says Melanie Underwood, a culinary educator and founder of Nourish & Gather. She warns that taking the human conversation out of cooking could further erode our cultural oral histories.

Context: Campbell's recent State of the Sides survey found that 27% of U.S. adults who celebrate Thanksgiving have used generative AI for holiday planning or cooking, up from 22% last year.

  • And 65% of shoppers say they would like to use AI in some aspect of holiday meal planning, per holiday shopper trend research from FMI, the Food Industry Association.
  • Among those celebrating at least one holiday this season, 34% say they'd use AI to find new recipes, 23% said they'd use it to plan the overall menu and 16% said they'd use it to make the holiday meal healthier.

Friction point: Food bloggers and chefs have warned that traffic to their trusted websites is plummeting with the rise of AI recipe summaries, forcing some to quit the game altogether. Plus, AI recipes on the "slop"-pier side can be disastrous for the dinner table.

  • The AI-generated recipes that pop up on Google's search results page "are often total nonsense," recipe blogger Eb Gargano told Axios in an email.
  • "They've been generated by AI – and, at least last time I checked – AI cannot cook a recipe or taste a recipe," she said. Food bloggers have a name for those recipes, she added: "Frankenstein recipes."
  • Underwood says she uses AI to help her with the operational side of her business. But when she recently asked a chatbot to scale her recipe for a large event and make a shopping list, it cut out ingredients — saying it was trying to improve her recipe.

Our thought bubble: AI is not a chef — while it's accumulated years of IRL chefs' knowledge, it can still lead you astray.

  • I asked ChatGPT to help me make my favorite Thanksgiving appetizers: stuffed mushrooms. I typically follow my mom's famous recipe (well, actually, Barefoot Contessa's, but shhh), but the AI-generated version differed in a few ways.
  • It wanted me to preheat to 400 degrees and bake for 20 minutes or so, while my family's go-to calls for a cooler 325 for 50. Chat's recipe opts for butter, while the Contessa's does not.
  • Some of the spices caught me off-guard as well: Red pepper flakes and thyme are not ingredients I usually throw in. To my untrained eye, the recipe still sounds tasty — but it's missing some of the key flavors in my dream stuffed mushroom, like sherry and scallions.

The bottom line: AI can be an inventive appetizer, but human execution remains the main course.

  • Underwood tells Axios: "AI has a place, but it doesn't replace human connection, and that involves even looking for recipes ... you can ask your friend as easily as you can ask AI."

Go deeper: How to make ChatGPT your sous chef

item.title: "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter": Democrats demand new restrictions on AI
item.description:
Prominent Democrats are calling for new restrictions on AI development following Axios reporting that employees at OpenAI and Anthropic increasingly fear their most powerful models cannot be safely released.

Why it matters: The political debate over AI is expanding beyond the economic consequences of the technology to a more existential question: whether companies should be allowed to build systems they may not be able to control.

  • The issue is gaining traction among Democratic leaders ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
  • Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.), a potential 2028 contender, outlined a playbook for AI regulations in an interview with "The Axios Show," noting that voters hate the technology because they fear losing control.

Driving the news: Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for immediate action:

  • "The people inside AI companies are sounding the alarm," Kelly said. "We built protections for nuclear weapons and other dangerous technologies, so why are we waiting with AI? We need safeguards and independent examiners in these companies, now."
  • "It is absolutely indefensible to say 'we will take this up next year' when the risks are imminent and the alarm is nearly universal," Schatz said.
  • "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter, and yet big tech refuses stop," Van Hollen said. "Inaction is not an option. Congress must step up."
  • Sanders went further, calling for a halt to advanced AI development: "The humans who are creating AI fear it could soon escape their own control," Sanders said. "Congress must act and pause advanced AI development NOW."

Catch up quick: More than two dozen sources familiar with internal debates at OpenAI and Anthropic told Axios that recent breakthroughs in AI capabilities have raised questions about whether future frontier models can be safely released.

  • Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models.
  • Some believe the problem is a technical one that's fixable.
  • Others believe companies should go a step further and stop training new models entirely.

The intrigue: As politicians debate how to ensure humanity retains control over AI, top industry executives are embroiled in a separate debate over how much autonomy humans should voluntarily cede to the technology as these systems become increasingly capable.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei personally pushed back Wednesday on a separate Axios story about views within the company that humanity will inevitably surrender some autonomy to superintelligent AI systems.
  • "No, I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do," Amodei said on X.
  • Amodei argued that AI must be governed by legitimate democratic processes.

Between the lines: Amodei's essay acknowledged room for nuance, highlighting that his views on human agency are mixed in specific instances where it could make sense for highly powerful AI systems to step in, like AI driving a car or designing a cancer drug.

  • Both Anthropic and OpenAI have acknowledged safety challenges and indicated a willingness to slow aspects of AI development or deployment.

What to watch: Whether concerns about losing control of AI become a defining issue in the Democratic presidential primary — and whether more lawmakers embrace restrictions on AI development itself, rather than just its deployment.

The bottom line: A debate that has consumed the people building the world's most powerful AI systems is spilling into national politics.

item.title: Anthropic CEO pushes back on Axios reporting on AI and free will
item.description:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives.

Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week.

What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said.

  • Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views.
  • He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency.
  • He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems.

The big picture: The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday.

The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products.

  • Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans."

item.title: The U.S. economy is ripping
item.description:
Wall Street has been reeling amid fears about the future of the AI boom. But in the here and now, the U.S. economy is experiencing an outright boom.

The big picture: Growth was even stronger this summer than it appeared, and the robust expansion is continuing this fall, according to a range of data released Wednesday morning. That is pushing Americans' incomes up and the pace of layoffs down.

  • The strong data helps explain why the Federal Reserve is prepared to raise interest rates two weeks from now even in the face of financial market turbulence.

Driving the news: The U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the second revision to GDP data — well above the 3.4% originally reported.

  • The strong results have continued into Q4. The Commerce Department separately said that personal income rose 0.7% in October, well ahead of analysts' expectations.
  • Overall orders for durable goods came in below forecasts for October, but core capital goods orders — a forward-looking measure of investment spending — climbed 1.2%, also well ahead of projections.
  • The Labor Department said that only 189,000 people filed new claims for jobless benefits last week, matching the lowest of 2026 and among the lowest readings on record (claims go back to 1967).

Zoom out: The Q3 GDP reading was powered by business investment, especially for software, showing that the AI buildout remains a powerful driver of overall economic growth.

  • It wasn't driven by volatile components of GDP like inventory and trade swings; real final sales to private domestic purchasers surged at a whopping 5.8% pace, and gross domestic income — conceptually similar to GDP — rose at a 4.4% rate.
  • Translation: This isn't some fluky reading, but rather a sign of underlying robustness.
  • Rapid growth looks set to continue in Q4; the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tool estimates current-quarter growth at 2.9%.

Zoom in: Nonresidential fixed investment — the GDP subcategory that covers capital spending — contributed 2.2 percentage points to overall growth in Q3. That was the highest since the bounce back following the 2020 pandemic. Excluding that episode, it was the highest since 2011.

Yes, but: Personal consumption expenditures rose a moderate 0.3% in October, below analysts' forecasts (+0.4%) and September readings (+0.6%).

  • That implies some softness in consumer spending, which, along with AI investment, has been powering the economy forward.
  • The silver lining, however, is that strong income growth paired with modest consumption growth is good news for American household balance sheets: The personal savings rate rose to 4.1%, from 3.6% in September.
Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

The strong growth readings affirm the Fed's all-but-certain plans to raise interest rates at a meeting concluding Dec. 9. Inflation data also released in the report shows why.

By the numbers: The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, which the Fed targets, was up 3.8% over the last 12 months, or 3.3% excluding volatile food and energy.

  • In month-on-month terms, both total and core PCE inflation came in at 0.3% for October, implying no meaningful deceleration is underway. The core number annualizes to 3.5% inflation.

State of play: While those readings were right in line with forecasts, they underscore that inflation remains far above the Fed's 2% target — as it has been for nearly six consecutive years.

  • The combination of rapid growth and elevated inflation looks more like a classic overheating economy — one in which the central bank needs to tighten policy to bring inflation into line.

Between the lines: The market turbulence of the last few weeks — the S&P 500 was down 2.8% as of 11:45am ET — points to risks that the AI investment boom may deflate in the quarters ahead.

  • But the Fed is unlikely to react to what might happen when growth numbers are coming in so hot and it has been missing its inflation target for so long.

What they're saying: "The economy isn't merely hanging in there," Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, wrote in a note.

  • "It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing, and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," he added.
  • "Boil it all down, and [Wednesday's] report reinforces an increasingly familiar tension: the economy is performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

item.title: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

The U.S. economy grew substantially faster this summer than initially thought, the government said Wednesday — a blockbuster upgrade to its estimate of third-quarter GDP.

By the numbers: The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate, up from the 3.4% initially reported and nearly twice the rate of 2.2% in the second quarter.

Why it matters: The economy has even more momentum than previously understood, a sign of remarkable resilience in the face of higher borrowing costs and stubborn inflation that could give the Fed more latitude to raise rates.

Zoom in: The upward revision reflected stronger business investment fueled by the AI buildout and software investment, as well as consumer spending.

  • A measure of underlying private-sector demand — which strips out trade, inventories and government spending — rose at a whopping 5.8% annual rate, up from the 4.9% initially reported.

The backdrop: Separate data out Wednesday showed personal income jumped 0.7% in October while inflation-adjusted consumer spending stalled, pushing the saving rate up to 4.1% from 3.6% the prior month.

  • The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — climbed 3.8% from a year earlier, from 3.6% in September.
  • Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, accelerated to 3.3% from 3.1%.
  • On a monthly basis, both headline and core prices rose 0.3%.

The bottom line: The U.S. economy was on remarkably strong footing heading into the end of the year, though inflation remains stubbornly high.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Trump prepares new round of tariffs on China, other U.S. trading partners
item.description:
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.

Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.

  • Post-election polling indicates voters overwhelmingly want tariffs to stay at current levels or decline. There's relatively little support — even among Trump's base — for them rising.

Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of a trade investigation that launched in March, The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.

  • China is the exception: The proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, on top of levies imposed under Section 301 in 2018. The rate is calibrated to preserve the nations' trade truce.
  • These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labor or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior U.S. official said.
  • The official added that the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to live up to its commitments.

Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.

  • The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15% tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties.
  • Vietnam and India would face tariffs of 20% and 17%, respectively, if trade deals are finalized.
  • On average, the proposals would raise existing tariff rates on targeted trading partners by roughly 5 percentage points, the official estimated.

The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.

  • The proposed tariffs are subject to a public comment period and hearings, with the levies taking effect as early as January, the official said.

What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs, China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.

  • The prospect of renewed tariffs weighed on global stocks, particularly Asian markets, overnight.
  • U.S. futures were sharply lower early Wednesday as well.

Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

  • The administration proposes raising tariffs on sugar imports exceeding existing quotas (regardless of origin) and imposing a 10% levy on previously exempt Brazilian aircraft, a U.S. official said.

The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting."
item.description:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, asserted in an interview with "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout. He said voters hate the technology because they fear losing control.

  • Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, told Mike Allen this week that after an "AI earthquake" helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control.

Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024. He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster.

  • Moore, Maryland's first Black governor, is a former Army paratrooper who deployed to combat in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, and was a Rhodes scholar and White House fellow.

What they're saying: Moore, speaking at the Maryland State House in Annapolis, makes it clear in this episode of "The Axios Show" that AI will be a huge focus of the 2028 presidential race after becoming a flashpoint in November's midterms. Among the governor's key points:

  • On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace."
  • On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots."
  • On whether regulating AI lets China win: "This is not a question of U.S. versus China. This is a question of man versus machine."
  • On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies."
  • On Nvidia and Trump: "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee. ... We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves making this decision."

Zoom in: Moore in September laid out his framework for AI policy, aimed at regulating frontier AI developers, shielding workers from surveillance and protecting children. His priorities include:

  • Ensuring regulations keep pace with rapidly advancing technology.
  • Holding companies responsible for releasing dangerous AI models.
  • Building on Maryland's efforts to protect people's name, image and likeness from AI misuse, including in political advertising. Earlier this year, Moore signed a law targeting deceptive AI in campaign ads, including images, audio and video.

The big picture: Governors across the political spectrum, from California's Gavin Newsom and New York's Kathy Hochul (both Democrats) to Utah's Spencer Cox and Florida's Ron DeSantis (both Republicans), are positioning themselves as filling the regulatory vacuum left by Washington.

  • Moore is linking AI policy to a broader Democratic message about corruption and the influence of money in politics. "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting," the governor told us.
  • "It's difficult to hear when Congress is talking about what they're going to do to protect us when we know that they are trading stocks."

Watch the episode ... Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube.

item.title: Most blame government for return of measles: Poll
item.description:
Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status, according to a new Ipsos poll. But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it.

Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress.

  • There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot.

What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks.

  • 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions.
  • There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans.

Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community.

  • There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%).

The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview.

  • A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats.
  • "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs.

That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation."

  • House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public.
  • They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response.

The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status.

  • It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases.

What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic.

  • Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024.

Methodology: The Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 20-23, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,022 general population adults age 18 or older.

  • The margin of sampling error is +/-3.2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

item.title: Rival AI leaders push back against Anthropic vision of surrendering human agency to AI
item.description:
Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a common view inside Anthropic: that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios.

  • That would put us on a slippery slope to forfeiting free will, critics say.

Why it matters: The debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models certain employees consider too powerful to ever release. Many see Anthropic as the first company that will confront these questions due to its lead at the frontier of AI development.

  • While critics have yet to call out the company by name, their public defenses of human agency and control take direct aim at what some have come to see as the worldview of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
  • When AI systems far surpass human intelligence, Amodei has said repeatedly that it will be preferable to turn over decision-making for "life-critical" cases to AI, and also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources.

Flashback: A product vision slide from several years ago that was revealed during litigation described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box."

The big picture: The thinking for Amodei and others is that once AI can demonstrably cure diseases, safeguard humans from harming themselves or prevent disasters better than any person, refusing to hand over control becomes irrational — or even unethical.

  • Proponents point to self-driving cars to make their case: Once statistical evidence points to autonomous vehicles being safer than human drivers, it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all, they say.
  • Inside Anthropic, a consensus has developed among some employees that humanity will — and in many cases should — safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions.
  • An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in many public remarks and that Anthropic trains Claude not to undermine human oversight.

Driving the news: Rival executives are increasingly rebuking the notion that humans will surrender agency, even as major math and reasoning breakthroughs convince insiders that superintelligence is imminent.

item.title: Oil's downward trend is pushing gasoline lower
item.description:
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

Brent crude is trading below $90 per barrel to start the week and briefly dipped to its lowest level since late August.

Why it matters: Recent declines should help gasoline prices keep falling. The average U.S. retail price is $3.61 per gallon, down nearly 70 cents over the last month, per AAA data.

The big picture: "The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz," ING analysts write.

Catch up quick: Qatar's prime minister met with Vice President JD Vance at the White House on Monday to discuss talks with Iran, according to Axios' Barak Ravid.

Reality check: Major risks remain, with the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region remaining a very dangerous place, so don't assume the downward trend will continue. And nothing is really back to normal.

  • The market intelligence firm Kpler finds tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was 42% below prewar levels in the seven days through Nov. 21, the WSJ reports.

Flashback: The International Energy Agency on Nov. 13 predicted the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter with supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict.

The bottom line: "The status quo is growing ever more bearish," Sparta Commodities' Aaron Kildow said in a note Monday.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: When reality shouts
item.description:
We naturally assume people in business and power are slightly full of it, spinning us wildly to exaggerate their achievements or capabilities.

  • In the case of AI and its ability to do irreparable damage to society, it's time for all of us — the media, the White House and Congress — to believe them: They've truly built something we don't understand and soon, if not already, can't fully control.

Why it matters: This is no longer a future problem. It's a today problem, if not a crisis.

You see this with near-daily glitches at airports or banks.

  • You see this in our reporting about two dozen researchers inside these companies claiming their AI is too powerful and uncontrollable to release.
  • And you see this in AI execs' own on-the-record warnings that we're at or near the point of the technology surpassing comprehension or control.

Just believe them. If we wait for a cyberattack on the U.S. electricity grid or some bad actor to release a pathogen at an elementary school, it's too late. We'll panic and make rushed, emotional decisions and bad policies.

  • It's not too late to prevent this, while still getting the upside benefits of AI.
  • In our conversations with hundreds of people involved in building and regulating AI, there's shockingly wide agreement about the dangers ahead — and ways to protect against the worst outcomes.
  • There's just no mechanism or urgency to bring the right mix of people together to do this.

The steps seem clear:

  1. Make this a society-wide, urgent call to action. This should be an all-hands-on-deck moment, the only topic Congress prioritizes short-term. Yes, it probably requires presidential leadership, and Trump is reluctant to slow things down. But his top cyber officials privately agree with us: This demands fast, smart, bipartisan action with heavy private sector involvement. Let 'er rip no longer feels like a plausible plan.
  2. Focus on safety and cyber first. Most leading AI companies would gladly slow down a bit, prioritize verifiable safety standards, and even accept government oversight with teeth if their rivals did. They'd also allocate money and time to help critical government agencies and businesses fortify software systems from cyberattacks. But someone, either Trump's AI team or the top leaders in Congress, needs to force them.
  3. Level with the American public. As a nation and as business leaders, we're doing a spectacularly terrible job of explaining this technology to the public. There's a reason that the most bipartisan topic in America is a shared loathing of data centers. People hate AI. Most simply don't see it as something that will make their life better. We need leaders who can discuss the good, bad and ugly of AI in real time, nearly every day. A society-wide project needs to involve society.

Go deeper ... "AI 2027: The reckoning."

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models are too unsafe to release
item.description:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios.

  • Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely.

Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers.

  • The rapid advances in reasoning across domains including math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have also made the models difficult, if not impossible, to contain or control in internal tests, the sources said.
  • Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.
  • This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us ... they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios.

  • "And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we've had at work up until now sort of go out the window."

Catch up quick: The power of unreleased models is already on public display.

  • An Anthropic mathematician used an unreleased "research" version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which had eluded the brightest human minds for more than 150 years. An unreleased OpenAI model helped generate proofs for hundreds of math problems.
  • Unreleased AI models were responsible for some of the industry's most shocking safety events, including the Hugging Face hack.

Zoom in: AI researchers have long contemplated a terrifying threshold: If an AI possesses superhuman capability, how could humans contain it? Training practices that make AI models faster and more capable — but present greater safety risks — are widening the gap between what models can do and how well humans can control them.

Problem 1: Reinforcement learning. A primary AI model training method — where models learn through trial and error by receiving rewards for passing various tests — is one of the techniques driving rapid improvements in AI capabilities.

  • Why it's scary: As AI systems get more capable, they become better at "gaming" their rewards, including bypassing safety guardrails if cheating leads to a higher score.

Problem 2: They know they're being watched. Historically, researchers monitored AI safety by forcing models to "think out loud" — writing out step-by-step reasoning before outputting a final action or answer. This transparency was a safety net, allowing monitors to catch rule-breaking or dangerous logic in real time.

  • Why it's scary: As models grow more advanced, they are internalizing that logic, arriving at complex conclusions while showing less of their work. Researchers say the most advanced internal models have shown patterns of hiding reasoning entirely or providing deceptive "cover story" chains of thought to satisfy human monitors, sources say.

Threat level: In public statements, top AI leaders have spoken about these risks.

  • "This is the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," CEO Sam Altman wrote on X, citing his chief scientist's proposal for industry-wide limits on AI development.
  • "The speed of development is quickly becoming too fast for us to keep safe," Anthropic's alignment lead wrote on X in September, quoting an essay from CEO Dario Amodei about pacing the frontier, a sentiment he reiterated when the company went public.

Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the implications of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will choose profits over safety.

  • Multiple frontier AI company employees said they feel executives have become out of touch with the severity of safety risks.

For the record: OpenAI has adopted new safety requirements that could slow the pace of model releases, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.

  • An Anthropic spokesperson told Axios: "Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe. Our responsibility starts in training and covers how we use models ourselves, not only what we release. ... The hardest safety work is still ahead, and we've been clear that we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us." The spokesperson noted delays to pretraining for a recent model to allow for more security.

What to watch: One solution some see is for frontier intelligence to remain within top AI companies.

  • Companies could allow outside access through product releases in enterprise work, science, math and other fields, without having to dole out wide access to the model's power, just as Anthropic and OpenAI did with the initial releases of their most cyber-capable models.
  • Many of the most concerned safety researchers warn that even internal testing and use of extremely powerful models is profoundly risky.

The bottom line: Those closest to the frontier are sounding the alarm. It's unclear who's listening.

item.title: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is harder than it sounds
item.description:
Reducing the Medicare eligibility age may strike Democrats as a realistic fallback to passing Medicare for All, but it's an option that would be incredibly difficult to pull off.

Why it matters: Even incremental steps to address affordability could have huge price tags and prompt fierce industry opposition.

Driving the news: Prominent Democrats have been throwing their support behind lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding children's health coverage and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits to Medicare.

  • Incoming Senate health committee Chairman Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for the package shortly after the midterms, calling it "an immediate first step to Medicare for All."
  • House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker in January, suggested on "Face the Nation" this weekend that Democrats may be able to work with Republicans on a package after President Trump said he may be open to working with Democrats.
  • Prominent Democrats in both the House and Senate have signed on to legislation that would lower the eligibility age to 50, though the bills are significantly different.

The big picture: Democrats' sweeping electoral gains have prompted weeks of discussion about what exactly a push to lower health care costs should look like.

  • The party is united in its desire to roll back the Medicaid funding cuts in last year's tax and spending law and to reinstate enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired late last year — lofty goals for any Congress.
  • There's widespread recognition that Medicare for All won't become law, and that Democrats aren't of one mind on a single-payer plan, with plenty of moderate members still loath to abolish private health insurance.
  • That tension has led to questions about alternatives, and whether "Medicare for More" could be an answer.

Between the lines: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would require a series of tough decisions.

  • Just shaving a few years off the current eligibility age could cost the federal government hundreds of billions of dollars.
  • To avoid adding to the federal deficit, lawmakers would have to come up with offsets that either generate equivalent revenue or, more likely, cuts to government spending.
  • Plus, the measure would likely attract intense and powerful opposition from health industries.

Zoom in: Lowering the eligibility age would almost certainly provoke strong blowback from hospitals and providers, which receive much lower reimbursement rates through Medicare than through commercial insurance.

  • "I think a general rule of thumb is the more people who are covered under Medicare relative to commercial or ACA, the less hospitals will be paid," said Marc Goldwein, senior policy director for the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
  • "From my perspective, that's not a bad thing," he added.

What they're saying: "You can't just add millions of people to Medicare without extra revenues, particular[ly] since the Medicare hospital trust fund already faces solvency issues," said KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt.

  • "Health care providers are likely to view lowering Medicare's age as — pick your metaphor — the camel's nose in the tent or a slippery slope," he added.
  • Hospitals fought former President Biden's 2020 calls to lower the eligibility age, fearing it would cost them billions of dollars in revenue.
  • "We believe expanding coverage to patients should not put their access to critical services at risk," said Colin Milligan, a spokesperson for the American Hospital Association. "Proposals that rely on Medicare would exacerbate chronic Medicare underpayments and threaten access to care and our ability to care for patients."

What we're watching: A serious legislative effort will also require answering crucial technical questions, like whether newly granted enrollees get the same access, benefits and premium structure as those 65-plus, or whether they'll be given the option to buy into the program.

  • Policymakers will also have to decide what to do about employer insurance — and whether employers could contribute toward Medicare coverage for their older workers.

The bottom line: The deeper you dig, the more complicated the policy gets.

item.title: Nvidia's one-man board: How Trump inherited Jensen Huang's scandal
item.description:
A euphoric Wall Street erupted Monday as President Trump personally secured Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, trading on the end of a scandal that — in reality — has only just begun.

Why it matters: By assuring Nvidia's board that Huang poses no national security risk, Trump has staked the credibility of the U.S. government on a CEO who lied about his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • It's among the most extraordinary presidential interventions in corporate history — a de facto bailout of the AI industry that will be scrutinized, in excruciating detail, by a hawkish and hostile Congress.

Zoom in: Six days after Nvidia's chairman publicly ruled out Huang's return, the board unanimously reinstated him after a secretive White House operation that blindsided even the company's top executives.

  • Trump joined Sunday's board meeting by phone, with one source telling Axios that the president pushed harder for Huang's reinstatement than Huang himself.
  • Nvidia acknowledged relying on assurances from "senior levels" of the U.S. government, even as its own investigation into the suspected Chinese espionage operation remained unfinished.

The market reaction was staggering: Nasdaq 100 futures surged to their 7% overnight trading limit, following a brutal week that had raised fears of a broader collapse in AI stocks.

  • Nvidia shares rocketed nearly 31%, adding hundreds of billions to the company's market value and helping Wall Street recover more than half of last week's losses.
  • Trump took a victory lap in an hour-long, freewheeling CNBC interview, declaring Huang "exonerated" and claiming the board ultimately "decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Screenshot via Truth Social

Between the lines: In orchestrating Huang's comeback, Trump drew on instincts that have defined own tumultuous political career — starting with his conviction that presidential power has "no limits."

  • Never surrender: Trump, the master of the political comeback, appears to see a fellow survivor in Huang. He made the comparison unmistakable by sharing a doctored version of his iconic 2024 assassination-attempt photo, with a bloodied Huang raising a red bra in triumph beneath an Nvidia flag.
  • Distrust of intelligence: Still embittered by the Russia investigation, Trump brushed aside warnings from his own intelligence agencies about suspected Chinese espionage at the heart of America's AI industry. Huang's allies appealed to that skepticism, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of the "deep state" and anonymous leaks.
  • The market is king: Trump viewed Huang's return as essential to restoring confidence in an AI industry worth trillions. For a president who treats stock prices as a measure of his success, Monday's spectacular rally offered instant vindication.

Zoom out: Trump's intervention transformed an already sordid corporate scandal into a political gift for Democrats, delivering a fresh target for the anti-corruption crusade that helped sweep them into power.

  • The backlash also cuts deep into Trump's own party and administration, where China hawks see the scandal as a direct threat to the technological supremacy they've spent years fighting to preserve.
  • Huang will face closed-door questioning alongside Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter next week, followed by a public Senate hearing Dec. 3 that promises to put the entire affair under a national spotlight.

The bottom line: Huang has reclaimed his throne, with the full might of the American presidency behind him. Like Napoleon returning from exile, the question now is how long he can hold it.

item.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia sparks bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill
item.description:
Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties.

Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January.

  • "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked in a social media post following the news.
  • "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in a statement to Axios.
  • "The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) posted on X.

Driving the news: The House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees have announced that Huang would testify next week. His reinstatement "changes nothing," an Intelligence Committee spokesperson told Axios on Monday.

  • "When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts."
  • The spokesperson added: "There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee's commitment to oversight."
  • Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate banking panel on Dec. 3.

What we're watching: Top Democrats say they will open their own investigations into Huang's reinstatement when they take power next year.

  • "Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said.
  • "We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight committee.
  • "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,"Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X.

Said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Finance Committee: "In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable."

  • Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told Axios: "We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC's access to our most sensitive technology."

What Democrats are saying: "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security," Schumer said.

  • Jeffries called for the annual defense authorization bill to include "ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries."
  • "The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom," Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said.
  • "Jensen Huang's reinstatement shows that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, our national security is for sale," Wyden said.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the top Banking committee Democrat, called the decision "reckless" and said the board still owes Congress "answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," adding that the Trump administration "needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

  • "Yet another example where, in Trump's America, the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard," Meeks told Axios.
  • Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), the top Democrat on the China Select Committee, called the decision "outrageous."
  • Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), a member of House Democratic leadership, blasted it as "irresponsible."

What Republicans are saying: "Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions," Curtis said in his statement to Axios.

  • "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
  • "Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking 'candor.' ... His behavior does not support reinstatement," said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), adding that he looked forward to Huang's testimony next week.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Monday morning that it would reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, president a board member after ousting him earlier this month.

  • The board voted unanimously for Huang's return.
  • The reinstatement comes after Trump repeatedly urged the board to bring Huang back.
  • Stocks saw an early, massive rally following the news. Huang's departure had sent the stock market into correction territory.

The bottom line: Both sides have a lot of questions. Democrats will soon have the power to get answers.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Sen. Kevin Cramer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Rep. Robert Garcia.

item.title: "Too big to fail": The economic fear behind Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback
item.description:
President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was "too big to fail" for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.

Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position.

Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios.

  • Huang resigned amid allegations he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and subordinates. The stock market's slump prompted President Trump and allies within the administration to push for his reinstatement.
  • "The President was pushing harder than Jensen," one source said. Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting Sunday night to argue for Huang's reinstatement, he told CNBC.

Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders.

  • A Trump adviser said allies sought to convince Trump that "deep staters" were working against Huang.
  • The intelligence included findings about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated to senior officials in a memo earlier this year.
  • A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was "mortified" when the memo leaked with his name attached.

Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips.

  • Despite the intelligence, Huang remained close to the president while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's inaction fueled tensions between him, Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and others.
  • A senior administration official argued the intelligence never established Huang was compromised, knowingly violated U.S. law or had sex with a spy.
  • "People are weaponizing some true information and spinning it to reflect as negatively as possible against Huang. That's the president's concern," the official said.

Vance's role

Trump and Vice President JD Vance viewed Huang as an important champion of open models offering Americans more control and lower costs than closed models like OpenAI's and Anthropic's.

  • The two were briefed on the national security concerns involving Huang and concluded they had not seen evidence of personal wrongdoing, the source said.
  • Anthropic has been warning the Trump administration that Nvidia's advanced chips power Chinese open source models closing in on the AI race.

Yes, but: These conclusions come as more and more connections between Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy Huang had an affair with — and the Chinese government and military come to light.

"He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said.

Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said.

  • Vance's Silicon Valley relationships helped the administration navigate the board's concerns, according to a source familiar with the discussions.
  • Keeping Huang as CEO was seen as the best option for national security, a source close to Vance said.

What we're watching: Huang's opponents in the administration now risk backlash from the president.

  • Bessent has been the loudest, criticizing Lutnick's inaction on TV and calling for the Nvidia board to find a new outside CEO and a "dramatic shakeup," but on Sunday softened his stance.

What's next: Trump's intervention settled the immediate fight over Nvidia's leadership but raised questions about the U.S. government's role in the board's decision.

  • Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to know which officials provided the national security input that Nvidia cited in reinstating Huang.
  • Three Republican-led House committees have scheduled interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2.
  • Nvidia says its independent investigations and cooperation with government inquiries will continue.

item.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
item.description:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not.

Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof. Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns.

What they're saying: "The Trump Administration's rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Schumer wrote Monday on X.

  • "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."
  • "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."
  • Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment.

The other side: White House spokesman Davis Ingle slammed what he described as "Trump Deranged Dumocrats and the Fake News' continued attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest" in a statement provided to Axios.

  • "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," Ingle added.
  • In an interview on CBNC, Trump said his "intervention was very important" in Huang's reinstatement. Asked what comes next for the company given the hit to Huang's credibility after his reported affairs, Trump predicted he'd "start off at an almost higher level," adding, "sex sells, fellas."

Driving the news: Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement as CEO, president and a member of the board Monday morning, less than two weeks after his resignation.

  • Despite saying last week that it did not intend to bring him back, the board did so anyway, amid urging from the White House.
  • Shortly after the announcement, Trump praised the board's decision, calling it "correct and proper," and saying "[t]he Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

Catch up quick: The whirlwind saga around the chipmaking behemoth was sparked by Huang's admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • The woman, Alice Huang, was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer that the Wall Street Journal reported arranged to send nearly $12 billion in top chips to Chinese companies.

Zoom in: "This underscores that enough people believe that our economy and national security are not just dependent on one company, but on one man," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser at the State Department, emailed Axios.

  • "I suspect this is being driven by last week's stock market drop and now it's clear that Nvidia sits at the center of an enormous web of deals and investments that appear increasingly dependent on one individual."
  • "From the standpoint of both democracy and healthy financial markets, no one person should wield that kind of influence. It is fundamentally corrupt."

Between the lines: Huang's resurrection also exposes the company to heightened liability and political turmoil.

  • He'll have to lead the company as it faces congressional and federal investigations.
  • But after his exit contributed to a sharp drop in tech stocks over the last two weeks, his return sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing.

What we're watching: How much appetite Congress has to expand its investigations into Huang and Nvidia after the stock market rallied significantly following his return.

item.title: Doctors who disagree with AI could face legal jeopardy
item.description:
AI could put doctors who disagree with it in greater jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, according to researchers who have tested some legal scenarios with mock juries.

Why it matters: The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there's also a baked-in assumption that it's never wrong.

  • That can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality.
  • Some may opt to order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability.

Driving the news: Researchers are using simulated malpractice cases to examine how much AI influences the perception of whether a doctor exercised "duty of care" in treating a patient.

  • The implications are significant: AI systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, and demand for tests is rising. But the systems invariably make mistakes.
  • Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology.
  • Physicians are demanding more protections. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients.

What they found: In a series of simulated court cases, researchers discovered that mock juries were more likely to side with the plaintiff in a malpractice suit when AI disagrees with a radiologist than when AI agrees with them.

  • One scenario involved a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage. When AI disagreed with the radiologist by flagging the condition when the radiologist didn't think there was one, the jurors sided with the plaintiff more often (72.9% of the time).
  • A second case was built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death. When AI was at odds with the physician by saying the patient had lung cancer when the doctor didn't think so, participants also sided with the plaintiff more often (78.7% of the time), the researchers wrote in NEJM AI.

Yes, but: A smaller percentage of jurors ruled against the physician when they were given data on the AI system's error rate.

  • Experts say that's significant because false positive readings are almost inevitable and can temper the belief that the technology is always right.

What they're saying: "We're uncovering an unintended consequence of AI adoption," said lead author Michael Bernstein, an associate professor at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. "AI can do a lot in radiology, but it's not all uniformly positive."

  • Bernstein said one concern is the prospect of more "defensive medicine," in which clinicians overcorrect and order follow-up scans and exams, which can drive up costs and patient anxiety.

Radiology is a closely watched specialty because AI is used extensively — and because missing an abnormality can be fatal. It's also among the fields with a high risk of being sued.

  • But research on perceptions of blame is cutting across many medical disciplines and underscores how physicians who are expected to rely on AI to cut down on medical errors still have to know when to override the systems.
  • "Because human operators are perceived as having control over the technology's use, responsibility unduly shifts to the human operator," Johns Hopkins researchers wrote in JAMA Health Forum last year.
  • They noted that physicians were consistently viewed as more liable than AI vendors, health systems that adopted the technology or regulators.

What we're watching: Bernstein and his colleagues found that double-checking AI results could reduce doctors' malpractice risks and prospective jurors' perceptions of whether a doctor met the "duty of care" standard.

  • The question is whether they can find the time.
  • The AMA is trying to shift the burden on AI developers and vendors — and pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data.

item.title: UN climate meltdown raises new doubts about talks
item.description:
The collapse of UN climate talks without an overarching deal is deepening doubts about the effectiveness of these summits — and bringing fresh calls for a shakeup.

Why it matters: Warming is on pace to far exceed the Paris Agreement target of holding long-term temperature rise under 2°C above preindustrial levels — and the more ambitious 1.5°C goal has slipped away.

🏃 Catch up quick: The COP31 talks in Turkey ended Sunday without a high-level "cover decision" of wide-angle agreements and goals.

  • Vulnerable island nations and the EU, among others, objected to a draft deal after some oil-producing countries blocked explicit endorsement of moving away from fossil fuels.

⚔️ Friction point: There was also pushback against proposed text that endorsed carbon capture as a major climate solution.

  • Finance discussions also disappointed advocates, with climate think tank E3G noting that "little or no new and additional money reached the table."

🏀 State of play: Sunday's events reinforce criticisms that the decades-old summit process — which birthed the 2015 Paris deal — is not suitable for spurring policies that meet the scope of the problem.

  • It could add urgency to years-long efforts to revamp how they work.
  • "I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here," Simon Stiell, the top UN climate official, said as the talks closed, per Reuters.

🥊 Reality check: Ending the practice that decisions require consensus — which effectively gives veto power to individual countries and blocs — would be a steep uphill climb.

Yes, but: There was some progress at COP31, per groups that track the granular talks.

  • For example, the climate group E3G cites procedural advances on the "Just Transition Work Programme," an initiative created in 2022 to support workers and communities in the energy transition.
  • And dozens of countries endorsed a pledge to bring electricity's share of global energy use up to 35% by 2035, compared to 23% today.

💭 My thought bubble: The failure in Turkey came just days after the U.S. Senate easily passed a permitting bill that would make it easier to build out renewables and fossil fuel projects.

  • Competing views on the COP process and the permitting bill among advocates show a wider tactical rift in climate and clean energy circles.

For many activists, COP31's meltdown shows a dangerous failure to confront planet-heating fuels, and that thwarting them must be a central, science-guided policy aim.

  • "In the same year that science warned we are on track to exceed the 1.5°C threshold, COP31 failed to face that reality head-on and name fossil fuels as the root cause of climate change," Bryan Bixcul of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change said in a statement.
  • But for other advocates, the real action is with duller, nitty-gritty steps (like permitting reform!) that help competitive clean energy grow faster, and anti-fossil fuel red lines are a distraction or even politically counterproductive.

What they're saying: "I may be too cynical but if this mess is what finally convinces people that it's not worth all this effort to get unanimous agreement on symbolic statements, maybe that's a blessing in disguise?" Columbia University climate economist Noah Kaufman posted on X.

What we're watching: Keep an eye out for any signs that the fracas in Turkey will bring changes to how these COP summits unfold.
