item.title: Behind the Curtain — AI 2027: The reckoning
item.description:
We've talked to more than 50 leaders in government, AI, business and cyber — from let-'er-rip AI accelerationists to shut-'er-down critics — and they were unanimous on one chilling assessment:

  • Cyberattacks on business and critical infrastructure will be constant, increasingly sophisticated and highly disruptive over the next 18 months.
  • These leaders describe 2027 as the year cyber becomes like weather: Outages will be frequent, disruptive, occasionally scary, and something people and companies must learn to navigate and live with daily. The chances of widespread disruption or real damage are rising fast.

Why it matters: We write this neither to forecast nor frighten. Rather, we're sharing what government and AI leaders say privately but won't say publicly.

The big picture: The disruptions of the past two weeks — from a global Microsoft outage to the FAA grounding air travel to a consumer banking glitch at Chase — were a mild preview of what experts expect is coming.

  • Bridgewater Associates, the world's largest hedge fund, put it bluntly in an assessment this month: "[We] are managing money based on a one-in-three chance of an economically destabilizing attack within the next year."

Horacio Rozanski, chairman and CEO of Booz Allen, calls this the "fog before the war" — a foretaste of greater chaos to come, when agentic invaders reach their full potential and can attack "at the speed of thought."

  • "Now is the time to take as many precautions as you can," Rozanski said. "Recognize that this is coming."

Most of these malfunctions appear to have resulted from companies and government trying to secure their computer and infrastructure systems against future large-scale cyberattacks. This pattern will persist.

  • Many future ones will be actual cyberattacks, carried out by U.S. rivals or smaller bad actors, using increasingly powerful AI to spot and exploit security vulnerabilities across society and our daily lives. Most top AI and government leaders expect at least small-scale strikes and fear much larger ones.

The best-case scenario described to us: regular, random outages and small-scale scares like losing bank access or air travel for a day.

  • The reason: Every government agency and company will mobilize to upgrade their software systems. So errors are inevitable.
  • These are assumptions based on private intelligence and an understanding of AI's capabilities, both to cause and fix glitches.

What worries top officials most: With thin AI expertise, an understaffed government and major companies are trying to keep pace with a technology that improves daily.

  • Even if government were loaded with competent experts, which it decidedly isn't, the sheer scale of vulnerabilities across federal, state and local government, not to mention all of business, would make it impossible to reliably secure.

Think of it as whack-a-mole with infinite moles.

  • Until this past month, the White House and Congress have focused largely on safety regulations and data centers, not imminent cyber risks. Now, even the White House's Super Intelligence Force (SIF) is scrambling to get its head around the rising risks while appraising near-daily reports of possible breaches.
  • And President Trump just ousted the White House national cyber director and named Kirsten Davies, who was the Pentagon's chief information officer, as the replacement. Davies has deeper subject-matter expertise than her predecessor, former RNC official Sean Cairncross.

Step back: Only by understanding the state of AI + cyber can government and business mobilize to prevent possible shutdowns across critical banking, electricity and water systems. This is our crack at distilling our conversations in a digestible way for Axios readers:

  • The double-edged sword. The good news: America's frontier AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.) built the most powerful AI on the planet, especially for building software. The bad news: AI that's great at building software is equally great at finding — and exploiting — its vulnerabilities, often called "bugs" or "holes."
  • The new dangers of old technologies. Government and business operate mostly on computer systems that were built for a pre-AI world. They're full of those bugs and holes. One vulnerability — exploited by a bad actor, or even triggered by someone trying a repair in good faith — can shut down an entire company or all air travel, as we just witnessed.
  • China foresaw this moment. A Beijing-sponsored hacking group, Volt Typhoon, has lurked in American critical infrastructure — water, energy, transportation and communications networks — for more than five years. A sister group, Salt Typhoon, broke into major U.S. phone carriers and took call records and wiretap data. The full number of compromised systems is unknown. The administration's view is that China isn't slowing down and the U.S. can't cede any advantage.
  • America is scrambling — and struggling — to catch up. Remember when Anthropic held back its Mythos AI model because of its breathtaking and scary cyber capabilities? Since then, some global companies, including JPMorgan Chase, have used Mythos and other technologies to locate and repair their vulnerabilities. Our intelligence agencies did the same. But most of government and American business haven't.
  • Cyber defense is costly. Lots of government agencies and businesses simply can't afford to safeguard their systems. The biggest companies can outbid others for top-tier cyber protection. The best firms are largely booked. Bluntly, many businesses hesitate to spend millions on pure loss unless they're convinced a threat is imminent.
  • The coming swarm. AI is getting better and better. And the ability of swarms of agents to act autonomously rises each week. Case in point: The FBI warned Nov. 13 about ARTEX — free, open-source software that lets hackers turn AI agents loose to run multiple phases of an attack at machine speed. The Texas energy regulator sounded alarms to the state's oil, gas and utility networks that they're a target. The EU warned governments about ARTEX after a 10-day cyberattack last month.
  • Government is divided and distracted. This is an all-hands-on-deck moment for society, and most of government is busy pointing fingers or looking elsewhere. Trump shows little AI expertise. Few people at the White House have a sophisticated understanding of the technology or are working to marshal government to prevent a hypothetical attack. Congress is no better. A random person at the bar understands this topic with the same depth as many lawmakers.
  • Wait and see. Oddly, although many officials with cyber smarts across different sectors or layers of government fear the same thing, they rarely talk to people about it outside their own domain and party. There's no real mechanism or institution to pull them together. Most just assume no serious preventive action will happen until a true mini-catastrophe hits. Yet they all assume that a mini-catastrophe is coming.

The reasons not to freak out: Everyone we talked to expects attacks. Few predict true catastrophe. There's a big gap between a bank going out for a day and a region going dark for a week.

  • A truly society-shaking attack, one that breaks pipelines or blacks out a region, still probably requires a nation-state. The actors who can do it, mainly China, pay the highest price if they do: An attack on the U.S. grid is an act of war, inviting a response against the assailant's systems.
  • America's fragmentation most likely isolates major incidents. Thousands of utilities and no single switch for the grid mean even a successful hit tends to stay regional.

So what could be done? The solution sits with the very first point of our distillation: We have the tech to both cause and fix this cyber threat. The government, through leverage or mandate, could pull the AI companies together and force them to help fortify vulnerable American systems before focusing fully on simply building more powerful models.

  • Top execs at the leading AI companies tell us they'd gladly comply if their rivals did. In fact, these leaders feel a sense of post-election urgency to act before a public event makes citizens hate AI even more than they already do.

Jay Clayton, chair of the White House task force, is finishing a voluntary safety regime for the big AI companies and is probably best positioned to pull AI CEOs together. He's well-versed in cyber and sees AI largely through a national security lens.

  • Other solutions will come from the private sector. JPMorgan Chase chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon is chairing an Alliance for Critical Infrastructure (ACI), a group of finance, energy, tech, telecom and airline giants aiming to "strengthen national resilience, reduce systemic risk, and sustain the continuity of the economy."

The bottom line: When we press all these leaders across government, business and AI, they agree that the chances of working together to prevent an attack are lower than the chances of an actual attack.

  • Go deeper: The chain-reaction era.

item.title: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
item.description:
President Trump said Saturday he'd gladly work with Democrats to cap interest and fees on credit cards, arguing that card companies simply make too much money now.

Why it matters: Though some argue capping rates would save consumers billions of dollars a year, the banking industry is equally adamant that it would deny credit to millions of Americans by making lending too risky.

Driving the news: Trump, in a Fox News interview Saturday morning, was asked whether a rate cap on cards was something on which he could find common ground with Democrats.

  • Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), poised to be the new chair of the Senate Banking Committee, is an outspoken advocate for such caps and has recently said she's ready to work with Trump to pass a bill.

What they're saying: "I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot — and the credit card fees that they charge. I'm all into it," Trump said.

item.title: Trump floats major tax on U.S. companies constructing data centers overseas
item.description:
President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do.

Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint, as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose.

  • As of December 2025, 4,000 data centers were operational, with almost 3,000 under construction or planned across the U.S.

What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials.

  • "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country.
  • Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes.
  • He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities.
  • "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it."

Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes.

  • Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally.

Context: Data centers ballot measures illustrate just how polarizing they've become in the past year.

  • Of the 53 measures on the ballot across 13 states through November 2026, voters favored limiting development in 52 cases, according to Ballotpedia.
  • Democratic challengers also successfully weaponized AI policy, ousting Republicans in Ohio, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania.

Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried: Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country.

Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S.

  • "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday.

Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence."

Go deeper: Voters deliver "AI earthquake," rebuking tech and billionaires

item.title: Anthropic is public, now comes the hard part
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

With its IPO done and dusted, Anthropic's shareholders will be watching its progress toward becoming a business that doesn't need constant capital infusions from investors and vendors.

Why it matters: Anthropic — along with OpenAI — is at the heart of the industry that's dominated the equity and debt markets for the last four years.

  • Much of the AI infrastructure boom is ultimately aimed at supplying computing power to these two companies.

Yes, but: The bill for that data center investment will start to come due over the next few years.

  • And Anthropic and OpenAI are going to have to pay for quite a bit of it.

How it works: Anthropic has covered much of its computing costs thus far by selling parts of itself off to compute vendors like Amazon and Alphabet, and by raising more cash from other investors.

  • But eventually the company's core business will have to generate enough money to cover those costs on its own.

Case in point: Anthropic's filings say it is on the hook for roughly $900 billion in spending commitments — mostly for data centers and computing power — with about half of that due before the end of 2030.

  • After the IPO, Anthropic is expected to have roughly $200 billion in cash and short-term investments in the bank, which should buy it some time.
  • But its sales will have to be a lot higher to just cover computing obligations, let alone the profits ANT's new shareholders are expecting.

By the numbers: As the chart above shows, Anthropic posted a loss of roughly $23 billion on revenue of nearly $17 billion in the third quarter.

  • It's true that much of that loss stems from a non-cash accounting charge of almost $22 billion.
  • But even the more favorable metric of operating income — which strips out the paper losses and gains that can obscure the company's core earnings power — still shows an operating loss of more than half a billion dollars in the third quarter.

The bottom line: Anthropic still has a long way to go before it is going to be standing on its own feet, financially speaking.

item.title: Medicaid expansion isn't a "slam dunk" for new Dem governors
item.description:
Democrats' sweeping electoral wins jump-started prospects for Medicaid expansion in red and purple states that rejected full expansions of the program under the Affordable Care Act.

  • But budget realities could make newly elected Democratic governors pump the brakes.

Why it matters: The changing of the guard sets up a test of whether states can expand coverage to more low-income residents right after Republicans in Congress weakened financial incentives for doing so.

  • States that are facing serious budget shortfalls and daunting cost projections already are signaling they may defer until conditions are more favorable.

State of play: Incoming Democratic governors in Wisconsin, Georgia, Texas and Kansas who campaigned on Medicaid expansion are now in a position to expand health coverage, and have more Democrats in their legislatures to help.

  • Wisconsin Democrats have arguably the most leverage now that they've captured the state Senate and Assembly in addition to keeping control of the governor's office. Plus, the state already covers adults with incomes up to the federal poverty level.
  • Expansion advocates in Georgia and Texas face a heavier lift, with Republicans still controlling at least one legislative chamber.
  • And in Kansas, the GOP lost its supermajority in the House, a key obstacle in past Medicaid expansion fights, but still controls both chambers.

Between the lines: Each state faces unique considerations. But one thing is true for all of the holdouts: The incentives for expanding aren't what they used to be.

  • Though the federal government still would pay for 90% of the expansion cost, last year's GOP reconciliation law made major policy changes and cuts to the program.
  • Expansion states now face stricter limits on provider taxes used to finance Medicaid, as well as on extra payments they make to hospitals and other providers to go beyond standard Medicaid rates.
  • They've also lost an important bonus: A temporary 5% increase in federal assistance for newly expanding states expired at the beginning of this year.

What's more, states will have to enforce new work requirements and document whether recipients perform 80 hours per month of work or other qualifying activities, or if they're subject to exemptions.

  • While the Trump administration delayed the requirements for six months, they aren't likely to go away.

What they're saying: "You're going to see a lot of [expansion] conversations start, but I don't think they'll be slam dunks. It's complicated and nuanced," said Matt Salo, a health care consultant and former executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors.

  • Incoming Wisconsin Gov. David Crowley already is acknowledging that reality and exploring alternatives for expanding coverage in the near term, including establishing a state-run health insurance exchange with a public option, per the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.
  • In Texas, some lawmakers are considering a "trigger" bill that would start an expansion only if the incoming Democratic majority in Congress succeeds in rolling back some of the restrictions in the federal law, the Texas Tribune reported.
  • Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms intends to pursue a full expansion next year, but also wants to streamline the state's existing limited expansion program, called Pathways to Coverage, as an interim strategy until full expansion is achievable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.

Democratic victories in the Texas and Georgia lieutenant governor's races still could boost Medicaid expansion prospects, since the lieutenant governor presides over the state Senate in both states and influences which legislation is considered, Max Reale, an analyst for Gordon Haskett Research Advisors, wrote in a note.

  • He pegged Wisconsin as the likeliest to expand its program and Kansas the long shot, since control of the governor's office alone failed to advance Medicaid expansion in past legislative sessions.
  • But cementing the four as expansion states would diminish the prospects of further Medicaid cuts under a GOP-controlled Congress and free lawmakers to pressure the six remaining holdout states to adopt expansion post-2028, Reale said.

What we're watching: New Democratic governors in purple states that already expanded their Medicaid programs could also pursue changes, said Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown's O'Neill Institute.

  • She noted that Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand promised to end the state's contracts with three Medicaid managed care companies due to high rates of improper denials of care, and to have Iowa's Medicaid agency or a nonprofit take over processing and paying claims.
  • Incoming officials in Iowa and Ohio could also go to court for relief from the most burdensome parts of the work rules, Keith wrote in Health Affairs.

item.title: Phoenix mayor walks fine line on AI boom
item.description:
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego wants more tech investment in her city — but on her terms, as data centers strain resources and frustrate residents.

Why it matters: Phoenix has become a bellwether for the AI industry's growing demands on electricity and water in an increasingly hot, resource-constrained world.

  • As the mayor, Gallego is navigating an outsized dilemma facing communities nationwide: How to embrace the AI boom while protecting residents and resources.

"I do want us to lead in technology, and I want us to be a tech-forward community," Gallego said at a recent event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios.

  • But she added: "I want companies who care about our community and will give back to it, and not just a race to see who can get the deepest incentives and the cheapest" power.
  • "We're open for business, but we're not for sale," she said.

Zoom out: Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies in her efforts to strike the balance she wants.

  • Democrats flipped both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs won reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966.
  • Affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate, Gallego said.

Catch up fast: Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity.

  • Now the debate is expanding from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return.

State of play: Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, has spent recent years trying to balance that.

  • She helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions. The state enacted a three-year pause on new applications this summer.
  • She opposes a blanket construction moratorium, favoring more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes.
  • Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules last year requiring special permits for new data centers.

Gallego says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they're built and what residents get in return.

  • That could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for neighbors affected by development.

By the numbers: Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said.

  • Many may never be built, but Gallego warned: "That's not a balanced economy, and that's not economically sustainable."

Friction point: Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over zoning restrictions adopted last year.

  • The city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court.
  • "We have been open and good partners to the industry, and it's deeply disappointing that they don't want to work with us," Gallego told Axios.

The other side: Developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values, entitling them to compensation under Arizona law, though industry allies have also acknowledged tensions.

Reality check: It's unclear whether Gallego can have it both ways: attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority.

Gallego is also navigating the tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat in the desert.

  • Newer cooling technologies can reduce water consumption at data centers but often require more electricity, shifting some of the water footprint to power plants.
  • "We're seeing many of these data centers get power from natural gas plants in an area of our state that is very constrained around water," Gallego said.

The intrigue: Data centers are adding another source of heat to a region already struggling with dangerously high temperatures.

  • An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit.
  • Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she's "jealous of Midwestern mayors" who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings.

What we're watching: Gallego worries Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain.

  • She compared the risk of abandoned data centers to Phoenix's vacant Kmart stores, many of which have been difficult to redevelop.

"What will I do in a community if we have these giant windowless boxes" that are no longer operating, she asked. "How will we redevelop or make them not become blight?"

item.title: Senate passes Trump-backed permitting bill
item.description:
The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill Thursday night that's designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects.

Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers.

  • Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors.
  • But critics argue the plan, which has White House support, would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes.

Driving the news: The vote was 62-33. The bill would still have to pass the House before the end of the year, and any differences would have to be worked out by both chambers before President Trump could sign it into law.

Catch up quick: It would make significant changes to federal permitting, including:

  • New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act.
  • Language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once they're issued, a priority for renewables groups and Democrats upset with Trump administration barriers.

State of play: There are also provisions to ensure that data centers pay for needed grid upgrades, and expand federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects.

Friction point: Many environmental advocates argue that the bill would dangerously erode safeguards in the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws.

  • Multiple tribal groups still oppose it despite changes aimed at easing concerns about consultation on historic preservation.
  • Energy and business groups, ranging from renewables developers to manufacturers to the oil and gas industry, are lobbying for the measure. The AFL-CIO and many individual unions back it, too.

What's next: The measure now heads to the House. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Bloomberg last week that he expects to have the votes to pass the plan.

  • Some Democrats have called for hitting the brakes, with some arguing they can write a better package when they control Congress next year.
  • Yet multiple backers within the wider Democratic coalition argue there isn't political space for an altered bill that President Trump would sign.

item.title: Retailers shake up Thanksgiving meal deals amid rising food costs
item.description:
Major grocery retailers are switching up their Thanksgiving dinner deals this year, with a few lowering prices, others swapping out items and some shifting toward more flexible meal options.

The big picture: Lower advertised prices from some retailers could offer relief to Americans already stretching their holiday budgets, but shifting menus mean shoppers may not be getting the same bang for their buck.

State of play: Higher fuel costs, poor growing conditions and other inflationary pressures have pushed up food prices ahead of the holiday.

  • The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for ten has increased 6% since 2025, totaling an estimated $58.63.
  • The increase is largely driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, the federation said.

Driving the news: Walmart is advertising a lower price for its Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, while offering 18% more individual items.

  • The retailer said this year's meal, which serves ten people for $35, is its "lowest priced one-click basket" ever, down from $39.93 last year.
  • The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish.
  • It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread. Fried onions were the only item to switch from name-brand to store-brand in 2026.

The other side: Aldi is also promoting a Thanksgiving meal $1 cheaper than in 2025, though several dishes have changed.

  • Instead of a 14-pound turkey, the 2026 dinner will have a 16-pound bird. It includes several sides, but not fan favorites such as mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese or green bean casserole.

Zoom out: Costco's gourmet Thanksgiving dinner is more elaborate than its cook-at-home grocery counterparts, with a similar menu and the same advertised promotional price as last year.

  • Both 2025 and 2026 dinners cost $199.99, serve eight people and include a five-pound turkey breast.
  • The prepared meal includes the same traditional sides and desserts, with the addition of candied yams. This year's dinner is marketed as 30 pounds, compared with 28 pounds in some descriptions of last year's offerings.

The intrigue: Kroger is shifting away from the fixed-price "Freshgiving" Thanksgiving meal bundle it offered in previous years. Instead, it is promoting individual holiday discounts and prepared foods in various portion sizes.

  • Kroger's chief marketing officer said the approach is intended to make holiday meals more convenient and accommodate gatherings of different sizes.
  • In 2025, Kroger advertised a Thanksgiving meal for 10 for under $4.75 a person, providing a 14- to 16-pound frozen turkey and traditional sides.

The bottom line: Your food preferences, guest count and budget will help determine if a Thanksgiving meal deal is the right choice for you.

item.title: Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%
item.description:
Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030.

Why it matters: Other tech giants have reported rising emissions as they race to build data centers, but Meta is going a step further by explicitly reconsidering its climate deadline.

Driving the news: The just-released sustainability report of the tech giant, one of North America's largest data centers operators, shows just how much growth in the AI industry is outpacing any efficiency gains.

  • Meta executives said they were "re-evaluating" the 2030 goal, first announced in 2020 when the company was still known as Facebook and before the generative AI boom.
  • They didn't specify what changes they're considering or when they'll make a decision.

By the numbers: Meta's electricity use jumped 35%, comparable to other tech giants. But Meta's emissions increase of 45% is far higher than its peers, Google (18%), Amazon (16%) and Microsoft (25%).

What they're saying: "When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned," wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability.

  • "The reality has been far more complex."

Zoom out: The race among tech giants to dominate AI is pushing their climate goals into the backseat, even as they continue investing heavily in clean energy.

State of play: Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal, though less than half that capacity is generating electricity so far.

The intrigue: Meta's report says it may turn to natural gas plants to power data centers when utilities can't deliver electricity fast enough — even though such projects are already underway.

  • It's also seeking to offset some of the methane emissions associated with its natural gas use by paying for cleaner gas production elsewhere.

Reality check: Meta's 45% emissions increase doesn't yet reflect the full impact of some of its biggest planned natural gas projects, suggesting its footprint could grow considerably more.

  • In Louisiana, utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas-fired generating units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts to serve Meta's data centers.
  • Separately, Ohio regulators approved a 200-megawatt gas plant built specifically to power Meta's data centers, while research firm Cleanview identifies a 521-megawatt gas project under construction for Meta in Utah.

Friction point: Meta's report was also revealing about water, a more immediate concern for many communities near data centers.

  • The company's direct water consumption fell 4%, but consumption in highly water-stressed regions rose 24%.
  • The estimated water consumption associated with generating its electricity — an often-overlooked environmental impact — rose 37% before accounting for its clean-energy purchases.

How it works: Natural gas plants typically use substantial amounts of water for cooling, meaning Meta's growing reliance on gas could increase its indirect water footprint even as its data centers become more water-efficient.

Yes, but: Meta is the only tech giant to disclose the water consumption associated with electricity, earning it high marks for transparency from Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who has studied AI's environmental footprint.

What we're watching: Meta's reconsideration of its climate deadline raises the question of whether other tech giants will eventually follow suit as the AI boom continues to strain their environmental commitments.

item.title: Why the Senate energy permitting bill might become law
item.description:
If the sweeping Senate permitting bill becomes law, it will reflect a rare convergence of political and market forces strong enough to trump the Beltway aversion to big, bipartisan deals.

Why it matters: The bill could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers.

  • Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors.
  • But critics argue the plan would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes.

The latest: A vote on final passage of the White House-backed bill could occur Thursday after the Senate plows through some more amendments.

The big picture: Many industries — pipelines, transmission, housing, you name it — call permitting a long bureaucratic and judicial maze that stymies projects.

Yes, but: That, on its own, isn't nearly enough to get this far. Here are other reasons the bill has a path to becoming law after years of failed efforts to upend permitting.

🗳️ The cost-of-living election. The midterms were soaked in affordability politics at a time of rising energy bills.

  • While critics can call the projected savings modest, cost is politically front and center.
  • The Rhodium Group estimates that big provisions it analyzed would cut average residential power prices by 3%-4% in 2035. Third Way, a group that favors the bill, supported the research firm's work.

📈 Rising electricity demand. U.S. power thirst has been rising in the last few years after staying largely flat for decades, driven partly by AI and wider electrification of the economy.

🦋 A maturing clean energy industry. As sectors like renewables and storage become more mainstream, "more developers and companies are seeing the real-world challenges" of doing projects, clean energy lobbyist Jeff Navin notes via email.

  • That puts them in agreement with utilities and oil and gas companies. "They all run into problems getting the permits needed to build energy infrastructure," said Navin, an Obama-era Energy Department aide and former Democratic Capitol Hill staff member.
  • Easier permitting is needed for transmission to carry the industries' power, as well as for building new generation itself.

😣 A mercurial White House was focused. The White House's National Energy Dominance Council was engaged with the bill.

  • Co-author Shelly Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) credited then-chief of staff Susie Wiles as a helpful player at the Sept. 30 bill rollout. Axios' Alex Isenstadt reported that new chief of staff Stephen Miller also wants a permitting bill.
  • Trump officials have also allowed some onshore wind projects bottled up by Pentagon reviews to proceed.

🔀 Shifting Democratic coalitions. Multiple analyses show the bill bringing somewhat lower power sector emissions compared to a world without it.

  • But when climate had more political juice a few years ago, a bill backed by oil industry groups probably would not have had this much Democratic buy-in.
  • Democratic co-authors and other supporters in the Dem coalition say easing the clean energy buildout is key to more climate progress in the future.
  • More moderate center-left voices and think tanks have new cachet, while environmental groups opposing the bill haven't made enough inroads despite longstanding ties to Democrats.

The intrigue: Data centers have been and remain a wildcard. There's a big political and public backlash, and opponents of the bill have seized on it, charging that the bill would help Big Tech by making the buildout easier.

  • But bill authors and backers are emphasizing language designed to ensure that data centers pay for grid upgrades and have higher transmission service costs.

What we're watching: The House. If it can pass the bill before the end of the year, there's a good chance the bill will get signed into law. If not, it's just another failed effort.

item.title: New alarm over China controlling drug supply chains
item.description:
China is intensifying efforts to control the entire drug supply chain, putting the U.S. at risk of being cut off from future lifesaving treatments, the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warns in a new analysis out Thursday.

Why it matters: Western drug giants have invested huge sums in Chinese biotechs to boost their product pipelines. But sharing capital and expertise could give Beijing more control over critical pharmaceutical technologies.

  • Concerns about the U.S. getting boxed out have intensified after the Chinese government proposed new restrictions last month on the export of certain technologies, including cell and gene therapy platforms.

Driving the news: Western drug giants are increasingly entering into licensing agreements with Chinese firms that redirect U.S. capital away from U.S. innovation and toward the Chinese pharmaceutical industry, the commission found in its analysis of 57 deals from the beginning of 2023 through last month.

  • The deals are being made earlier in the drug discovery process, allowing the Chinese partners to gain not just capital but know-how in developing and commercializing treatments.
  • This kind of knowledge transfer in automobiles, semiconductors and industrial chemicals gave Chinese industry a competitive edge and leverage to control global markets for the products, according to the commission, which was established by Congress to examine how emerging biotech intersects with national security.
  • "The end game is the same for the [Chinese Communist Party] in the pharmaceutical industry," the commission warns, saying the goal is increased U.S. dependence on Chinese innovation and enrichment of the Chinese pharmaceutical industry.

Between the lines: Drugmakers including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer have been drawn by China's surge of investment in the life sciences and the promise of faster clinical trials and product approvals.

  • Typically a Chinese biotechnology company sells the license to develop or commercialize a treatment it developed to a multinational pharmaceutical company.
  • The Western companies see the arrangements as a way to outsource the burden of drug discovery and verify early results. But the commission found that the deals are increasingly based on preclinical data and that upfront payments are coming earlier in the R&D cycle.
  • The commission says this can result in a "flywheel effect" that sees royalties and equity in joint ventures flow back to China, fueling new research and infrastructure and attracting global talent.

What they're saying: "The CCP seeks dominance in biotechnology as a source of economic power and geopolitical advantage, and Beijing has spent decades pursuing a deliberate strategy to achieve that at all levels of the value chain," said commission executive director Caitlin Frazer.

  • "U.S.-China pharma deals are starting to favor the Chinese startups, which risks eroding biotech R&D in the U.S. This trend should be alarming for policymakers."

Threat level: The concern is what happens if China scales up and corners a market, establishing a stranglehold on supplies of key products and ingredients.

  • That's especially critical in pharma. While a chip shortage may result in delays replacing a car or phone, a drug shortage delays treatments for controlling seizures, treating infections or managing severe pain, Brookings Institution senior fellow Marta Wosińska has noted.
  • In a report last year to Congress, the commission posed a hypothetical scenario in which Beijing withheld a breakthrough treatment from American patients in the event of a conflict in Taiwan.

State of play: Last month, the Trump administration proposed subjecting certain deals with Chinese life sciences companies to new screening requirements or prohibiting them altogether.

  • The administration cited the risk of "outbound investments" being used to create biological weapons or brain-computer interfaces for surveillance, or to make U.S. supply chains overly dependent on a country.
  • Cash-based deals that bring royalties and milestone payments are still permitted, but equity investments in Chinese firms would be prohibited and certain joint ventures could also be targeted, per a Sidley analysis.

The commission, in its new analysis, calls the proposal "a prudent step to curtail China's biotechnology ambitions" but adds policymakers "must act now to empower the United States to out-innovate strategic competitors before it's too late."

  • Pharma and biotech interests have been pressing Congress and the administration to take steps to update and streamline U.S. drug development, improve patient access to clinical trials and pass stronger patent protections.

What we're watching: Whether this week's meetings between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping yield new agreements on strategic technologies like biotech or lead to tighter export controls.

item.title: Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO)
item.description:
Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective:

My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be?

The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously, but I'm not in panic mode.

  • When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it.
  • A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions.

Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves.

  • But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill.
  • We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing.

Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place.

  • There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems.

Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team.

  • I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve.

The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping."

  • I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do.
  • I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.

item.title: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
item.description:
Anthropic will make its Wall Street debut Thursday at a moment of profound contradiction in the history of AI:

  • The humans are embattled — bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil and political revolt.
  • But the machines are ascendant — accelerating toward an "intelligence explosion" they expect will transform civilization.

Why it matters: The industry's recent chaos has obscured a breathtaking surge in technological progress, forcing some of the world's leading researchers to reconsider just how soon AI could surpass human intelligence.

Zoom in: Inside Anthropic, soon to be valued north of $1 trillion, independent researchers at METR found that AI models are advancing at nearly twice their historical pace — largely fueled, they believe, by AI itself.

  • Anthropic's own data shows Claude went from leading fewer than 1% of the company's AI research tasks in February to more than a quarter by August, with humans still supervising.
  • METR found no clear obstacles to sustaining this pace over the next year, and reviewed confidential evidence suggesting the acceleration itself may be gathering speed.

Zoom out: Across the frontier, leading companies are racing up what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls "the exponential."

  • OpenAI disclosed Tuesday that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement — equivalent, the company says, to giving every researcher another highly capable engineer.
  • The advances span both software and silicon: OpenAI says its models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months, while Google's Gemini is reducing weeks of chip-layout work to hours.

The big picture: These breakthroughs are pushing some of AI's top forecasters to shorten their timelines for the fabled "intelligence explosion" — a runaway cascade of self-improving AI that could propel machine intelligence far beyond human comprehension.

  • The influential AI Futures Project now expects machines to surpass the world's best human AI researchers next year, a dramatic revision driven largely by METR's findings at Anthropic.
  • Paul Christiano, an AI safety pioneer who recently joined OpenAI's board, puts the odds of superintelligence emerging within a year at one in three if development continues at its current pace.

Between the lines: For all their extraordinary capabilities, the machines remain at the mercy of a fallible human race.

  • Take Nvidia: Jensen Huang's sex scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis at the very height of its technological and financial power, endangering virtually the entire AI ecosystem.
  • AI leaders' disastrous messaging, veering between promises of utopia and warnings of mass unemployment, has poisoned public trust and helped fuel a revolt against data centers.

Meanwhile, the industry's enormous capital requirements, increasingly tangled financial arrangements and intensifying U.S.–China chip war threaten to impose limits that the technology itself has yet to encounter.

  • Then there's the question of control: Months after OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face, the company acknowledged Wednesday that it still cannot fully rely on AI behaving as intended to prevent harm.
  • One of the industry's biggest gambles is that AI itself will help solve the problem of controlling future superintelligence. "You're building the plane as you fly it," Christiano told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel this week.

The bottom line: Anthropic's historic IPO captures the central contradiction: Investors are betting on nearly limitless technological progress, while the industry's future remains hostage to distinctly human failures.

item.title: Exclusive: Bots amplified conspiracy theories and panic about recent tech outages
item.description:
Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the outages and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups.

  • While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic.

Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week.

  • Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs.

Yes, but: There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online.

  • Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities to make software more resilient.
  • Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported.

By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics.

  • During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts.
  • Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts.
  • Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about Bank of America's outage and 28% of posts linking Chase's outage to other disruptions.
  • PeakMetrics analyzed social media discussions surrounding six recent outages and classified accounts that were likely to be bots and conspiracy-related posts.

Threat level: Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that it sees some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments.

  • PeakMetrics also observed a "small number of foreign state media and state-aligned accounts in the conversation," Pratt added.

Zoom in: The most popular theory being pushed was that each of these incidents must be connected.

  • More than half of posts about Chase's outage linked it to other recent disruptions, including the FAA ground stop and Microsoft's outage.
  • A fabricated statement attributed to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon fueled speculation that North Korean and Russian hackers were behind the banking outages.
  • During Microsoft's outage, suspected bots circulated identical posts linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure and banking outages in Japan and Paraguay.

The big picture: Foreign influence operations have historically used bots to amplify political grievances and spread false narratives, but it's unclear who's operating the accounts pushing theories about the latest outages.

Between the lines: The longer outages dragged on without clear explanations, the more room conspiracy theories had to spread.

  • During Microsoft's outage, speculative posts nearly tripled on the second day, when the disruption had stretched beyond 12 hours.
  • By then, nearly 1 in 5 posts offered an alternative explanation for the outage, according to PeakMetrics.

The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that "it's unclear if [the outages are] all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity." Jeffries said he wants briefings for lawmakers in both chambers.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters that it would be "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if these outages aren't connected, according to NBC News.

What we're watching: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them.

item.title: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
item.description:
Anthropic on Wednesday raised over $81 billion in a long-awaited IPO that valued the Claude maker at over $1 trillion.

Why it matters: Wall Street expects the AI boom to continue, despite some recent tumult.

Zoom in: Anthropic priced at $83 per share, well above its planned range of $70 to $78 per share.

  • It imputes an initial market cap of $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value of around $1.5 trillion.
  • Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares, but increased it to 980 million shares.
  • The company also could raise significantly more money if underwriters exercise their so-called "greenshoe" option, while Anthropic also will receive $26 billion via a concurrent private placement from tech giants like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft.
  • Allocation decisions were expected to last several hours on Wednesday evening.

Context: Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its most recent private round. The apples-to-apples comparison would be with the fully diluted value.

  • SpaceX is the current IPO record-holder having raised $86.25 billion, although that included the greenshoe.

What we're watching: Shares are expected to begin trading Thursday, Nov. 19, on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT."

item.title: Trust, but prepare: How to make sense of AI's age of upheaval
item.description:
Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related.

  • So what the hell is going on?

The most likely answer: This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once.

The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems.

  • The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering.

  • They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems.
  • The catchphrase gaining currency: "Software Beirut" — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better.

What this means for YOU: Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire.

  • It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking.

You should also prepare: Reset and protect your passwords. Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. 

  • Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared.

Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns:

1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's nationwide airspace outage was simply a case of replacing old copper wires with new fiber that went very, very badly.

  • Aging infrastructure can struggle to accommodate new components. In this case, a network problem overwhelmed legacy equipment, triggering a cascade that grounded flights across the country.

2. AI spotting bugs and humans rushing to fix them: This is one of cyber expert Nicole Perlroth's core scenarios, which went viral this week. AI can find vulnerabilities faster than humans can investigate and patch them. In the frantic sprint to fix those weaknesses before hackers exploit them, systems can break.

  • According to the Washington Sun, banking executives and NSA officials have told lawmakers that rushed efforts to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities contributed to some of this week's outages.

3. Bad actors attacking vulnerable systems: Across Europe, supermarket refrigerators are being hacked, spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

  • No one had "protect the fridges" on their security to-do list this year. But the attacks show how hackers can exploit even the most mundane internet-connected systems — with devastating real-world consequences.

4. AI enabling new forms of cyberattacks: Google said this week it had identified, for the first time, bad actors using AI to find weaknesses and launch cyberattacks entirely on their own — with no human in the loop.

  • If it wasn't already clear, Google warned that "the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point."

The bottom line: Most companies and much of government are woefully unprepared for the new era of AI-powered cyberattacks.

  • Their systems are old, clunky and riddled with vulnerabilities. Fortifying them will take enormous amounts of money, time and persistence.
  • The good news: We can see the danger coming, and still have (a little) time to protect ourselves for what may come next.

Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Zachary Basu contributed.

item.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
item.description:
Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive.

Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost.

  • This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab.
  • The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year.

State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data.

  • There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic.
  • That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year.

The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits.

  • He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving.
  • Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less.

How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied.

  • EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals.
  • There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year.

The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes.

  • "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

item.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
item.description:
The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease.

Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat.

Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected.

  • That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times. (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.)
  • Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized.

State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease.

  • Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC.

Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children.

  • But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months.
  • The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months.
  • Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life.

What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X.

  • "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks."
  • Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended.

Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally.

  • "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.
  • Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added.

Zoom in: New research has also documented how measles infections acquired during pregnancy are becoming more common and can have dire consequences.

  • Between January 2025 and the end of September this year, 112 cases of measles during pregnancy — almost entirely among unvaccinated women — and 13 cases of congenital measles (meaning a case in a newborn contracted from its mother) were reported to the CDC, according to research published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine.
  • Nearly a quarter of the pregnant women were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, and adverse outcomes for babies delivered within 14 days of their mothers developing a measles rash included preterm delivery and admission to intensive care.
  • Congenital measles can also result in severe neurologic complications, the report notes.

The bottom line: "We will likely be dealing with measles this year, next year, and the year after," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, wrote on Substack.

The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease.

Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat.

Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected.

  • That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times. (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.)
  • Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized.

State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease.

  • Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC.

Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children.

  • But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months.
  • The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months.
  • Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life.

What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X.

  • "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks."
  • Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended.

Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally.

  • "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.
  • Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added.

item.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
item.description:
A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock, breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders.

Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime.

  • Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed.

Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks.

  • The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.
  • In a separate report Friday, Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks.
  • Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex.
  • Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector.
  • CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month.

Reality check: Cyberattacks are still scary, and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks.

  • A litany of popular services — including Microsoft, Apple, Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week.
  • An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI. Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now.

What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios.

  • "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added.
  • Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios.

How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves.

  • A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network.
  • AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points.
  • The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision.

Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks.

  • Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power.

The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter.

  • Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect.
  • But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them.
  • He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene.

What we're watching: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

item.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
item.description:
Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week.

Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen.

Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking or a kind of cyber apocalypse.

  • To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have more to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as institutions try to safeguard their systems from a potential hacking onslaught.
  • Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented.

Driving the news: National security officials and Wall Street executives have told lawmakers the outages stem from efforts to fix software bugs found by AI systems, according to The Washington Sun.

  • Global institutions are in an all-out race to avoid a "bugmageddon," a scenario in which AI-assisted hackers are able to find and exploit vulnerabilities across the internet before they can be fixed.
  • Apparently, that process has created its own instabilities.

Catch up quick: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday.

  • United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
  • Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services.
  • Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages.

Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones.

  • Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks.
  • United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment.
  • Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.

Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking.

  • Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed.
  • That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say.
  • AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible.

What they're saying: Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios.

  • "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says.
  • "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology."
  • "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right."

By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios.

  • However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five.

The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame.

  • "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI."

Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked.

  • That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover.

The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected.

  • When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns.

Editor's note: This story was updated to offer additional detail on potential causes of recent outages.
