item.title: Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton's FDA nomination
item.description:
The White House is dropping Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

  • "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday.

Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August.

  • She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda.
  • Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone.

The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee.

  • Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying."

What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said.

  • The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation.

What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday.

  • The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

item.title: Exclusive: Donald Trump Jr. signals investors underestimated AI pushback
item.description:
Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York.

The big picture: The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers — which President Trump rallied around.

Driving the news: Trump Jr. asserted that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But he added "that doesn't mean it's not real" in an interview with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack Tuesday.

  • "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," he said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'"
  • Asked by Primack if investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said, "I think we saw that very clearly."
  • He likened AI to other "any great innovation," but said, "This is gonna be one of those things, but it is going to take some time for people to learn how to adapt that into their regular lives."

State of play: Trump Jr. spoke with Primack alongside 1789 Capital co-founder Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024. The investment firm has since exploded from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions.

Zoom in: Trump Jr. agreed that the rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence.

  • That public anger is becoming key to candidates: Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi.
  • Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom. While Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will tackle the tech moving forward.

Zoom out: Asked if there was anything Democrats and the White House could agree on after a November shellacking that could be good for business, he said "we've got to focus" on costs and inflation.

  • But he argued that "the second they win ... it's about investigations" — which Trump Jr. could find himself targeted by.

Editor's note: This story was updated with additional context throughout.

item.title: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
item.description:
Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward.

Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital.

What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said at the end of a conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

  • She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check.
  • "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added.

In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds.

  • Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world."
  • CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each jumped in after-hours trading.

Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly.

  • Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said.
  • The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make."

Catch up quick: Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence.

  • She was also an executive with a major Nvidia customer that allegedly helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country.

On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones threw cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said.

  • The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

item.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
item.description:
Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.

  • On the company's earnings call, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," despite a movement among some employees and investors to bring him back.

Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit.

Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.

  • S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion.
  • The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion.

The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.

  • The stock was up as much as 5% in after-hours trading Tuesday following the company's earnings call.

It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.

  • On the earnings call, she struck a steady tone, saying the company's momentum and innovation remain substantial.
  • "We've got this," she said.
  • Kress didn't mention Huang by name on the call but acknowledged the turbulent time and the "diverse" opinions — an apparent reference to the campaign to bring back Huang.

What we're watching: WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company.

  • An SEC spokesperson declined to comment.
  • Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the executives didn't discuss it on the call — but they said their quarterly 10Q filing with the SEC will be delayed.

The earnings call came hours after Huang posted a public letter saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO.

  • Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders.
  • Jones said the company would not take questions on Huang's exit. He said the board would consider external and internal candidates and wants to move "as quickly as possible" but won't make a move until it finds "exactly the right person."

The intrigue: Huang reportedly faced pushback from Kress as he pushed financing deals to backstop the AI ecosystem.

  • On Tuesday's call, Kress signaled that the company would continue to provide financing where appropriate but would be "selective" and ensure that guarantees are necessary.

Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress made on the company's earnings call.

item.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
item.description:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag.

Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop.

  • Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop.
  • "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion."
  • Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday.

Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch.

  • "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters.
  • Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the "Big, Beautiful Bill" last year.
  • "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said.

Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds.

  • "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday.
  • Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process.
  • But Democrats are also expressing skepticism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't."

The intrigue: Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab.

  • "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters.
  • "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said.
  • "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

item.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop, the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday.

Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country.

Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed.

  • The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections.
  • The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition.

The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers.

  • Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas.
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause.

What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement.

  • "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them."

Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so.

  • "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.
  • "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed."
  • They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned.
  • The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23.

The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands.

  • "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said.

By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter.

  • Just 69 are operational.
